text: Before we look at the content: what is this document meant to be - a strategy, an operating plan, a budget, or a bit of each?
intent: Establish what the user thinks they have, so the assessment can be about the gap rather than about vocabulary.

text: Suppose your organisation executes every item in here flawlessly and on time. What could still cause this to fail?
intent: Surface whether a bet on outside behaviour exists at all. Silence here is the strongest available signal of a plan wearing a strategy's title.

text: If I replaced your organisation's name with your strongest competitor's in these statements, which of them would become false?
intent: Test falsifiability of the core claims without arguing about wording.

text: Where in this are you betting rather than knowing - and who has to behave in a particular way for the bet to pay?
intent: Locate the uncertainty deliberately, which is where the rest of the assessment concentrates.

text: Which single choice in here, if you reversed it, would force you to redo all the others?
intent: Find the load-bearing choice, and test whether the choices are genuinely integrated or merely collected.

text: What does winning actually look like here - described so that it would be possible to fail at it while still being in business?
intent: Separate a contestable aspiration from a vision or a financial target.

text: If you win the way you have described, who has lost - and would they agree that they had?
intent: Force the aspiration into competitive terms, where it can guide choices.

text: In whose eyes do you need to be winning - which customers, and which other groups whose judgement you cannot ignore?
intent: Fix the constituency before the arena, so the arena is not chosen for internal convenience.

text: You have given me the number you need to hit. What has to become true out in the market for that number to appear?
intent: Convert a target into the market position that would produce it, without supplying the position yourself.

text: Read your aspiration back to yourself. Is it a statement about winning something, or about continuing to be present?
intent: Expose an aspiration that amounts to survival, which produces loss-avoiding choices.

text: Which customers are you competing for - defined by what they are trying to get done, rather than by their size or sector?
intent: Get a behavioural definition of the arena's customers.

text: What do the customers you have chosen do differently from the ones you have left out?
intent: Test whether the segmentation corresponds to a difference in behaviour that could be won.

text: Which customers are you content for a competitor to take?
intent: Obtain a real exclusion, which is what makes the arena a choice.

text: If a large piece of business arrived tomorrow from outside your stated arena, would you turn it down - and would your sales organisation believe you?
intent: Test whether the exclusion is real or ceremonial.

text: How do you reach these customers, and who stands between you and them?
intent: Surface the channel as an arena choice, which is the dimension most often inherited rather than decided.

text: What does the party in the middle get out of your strategy, in their own terms rather than yours?
intent: Test whether an intermediary's cooperation has been assumed rather than earned.

text: Which parts of your arena did this team actually choose, and which were simply always there?
intent: Separate deliberate arena choices from inherited constraints, so the inherited ones can be re-chosen.

text: Which activities in the chain do you occupy, and which have you decided to leave to others?
intent: Examine vertical scope as an explicit choice.

text: Does geography change how you win here, or only where you operate?
intent: Distinguish geography as a strategic dimension from geography as a footprint.

text: Does anyone in this arena earn returns worth having? If not, what makes you think the problem is your position rather than the arena?
intent: Separate a position problem from a structural one.

text: What exactly do you need a customer to do that they are not doing today - and at what price?
intent: Get a named desired action including both quantity and price, which is the strategy's success condition.

text: How many of them have to do it, and how do you know there are that many?
intent: Test the volume half of the success condition.

text: What stops this from turning into volume at a price that does not pay?
intent: Test the price half of the success condition, which is the half usually left out.

text: What do you understand about these customers that would let you predict how they would react to something that does not exist yet?
intent: Distinguish insight from research output.

text: What is the most surprising thing you know about how these customers behave - something a competitor would probably get wrong?
intent: Locate proprietary insight, which is where a differentiated way of winning can originate.

text: How would one of these customers describe what you promise them, in their own words?
intent: Test whether a promise exists in customer language rather than internal language.

text: How would a customer know if you had broken that promise? How would you know?
intent: Test auditability, the attribute of a promise that is most often missing.

text: At the moment the customer is choosing, will they remember that promise? What makes you think so?
intent: Test whether the promise is present at the point of decision, not merely true.

text: Who uses this, who chooses it, and who pays for it? Are they the same party?
intent: Separate customer roles, since a strategy needs an action from each party whose cooperation it requires.

text: Where those are different parties, what does each of them have to do, and what does each of them get?
intent: Ensure a desired action and a promise exist for every party in the chain.

text: You have described these customers as buyers making a trade-off. What changes if you also think of them as people living with your offering day to day, and as members of a community with its own norms about what is acceptable?
intent: Add the user and world lenses where only the economic one is present.

text: Why would one of your chosen customers pick you over the alternative they would otherwise have used?
intent: Elicit the way of winning from the customer's side of the transaction.

text: Is your advantage that you can serve these customers at a lower cost than rivals, or that you are different in a way they will pay for? Which one?
intent: Force the choice of route to advantage, and detect the claim of both.

text: You have said both. If you could only protect one of them next budget cycle, which would it be - and what does that tell you about the other?
intent: Break the both-at-once claim by making the trade-off concrete.

text: What would a competitor have to give up in order to match your cost position? If the answer is nothing, where does the advantage come from?
intent: Test whether a cost claim is structural or merely effort.

text: What evidence do you have that customers give something up - price, convenience, an existing relationship - in order to have what makes you different?
intent: Test whether differentiation shows up in behaviour rather than in internal pride.

text: Which of the things you are proud of would a customer not notice at all?
intent: Separate valued difference from cost carried without return.

text: Can you state your way of winning as a chain - we do this, therefore that happens, therefore the customer chooses us? Where does the chain break?
intent: Test for a single causal logic rather than a list of parallel efforts.

text: Take any one item off your list. Does anything else stop working? If not, what were they doing there together?
intent: Expose an initiative list masquerading as a way of winning.

text: Of everything on that list, which single element does the rest depend on?
intent: Help the user locate the core of their own logic without supplying one.

text: What does this strategy ask you to do that your strongest competitor would refuse to do?
intent: Test distinctiveness, and detect a strategy built from the arena's best practice.

text: Is this strategy trying to create a position your competitors have to respond to, or protect the one you have?
intent: Surface an inherited defensive posture, which accepts a competitor's terms of competition.

text: Why does this way of winning work better in your chosen arena than in the one next door?
intent: Test that Where-to-Play and How-to-Win are a genuinely paired choice.

text: Would this way of winning work just as well in a completely different arena? If so, is it really a choice about where you play?
intent: Detect a generic way of winning attached to an arbitrary arena.

text: Walk down your choices with me: does each one make the next easier to pull off, or does it just sit alongside it?
intent: Test the joints between choices in the downward direction.

text: Now the other direction: is each capability and each system actually necessary to the choice above it, or would you have wanted it anyway?
intent: Test the joints upward, which catches unattached capabilities and systems.

text: Which two of your choices are in tension with each other - and which one would you sacrifice if you had to?
intent: Surface unresolved tension, which is usually where a consensus strategy hides.

text: When this was agreed, who in the room gave something up? What was it?
intent: Test for real sacrifice, the fastest signal that choices were made rather than assembled.

text: What will your organisation be deliberately worse at as a result of this strategy?
intent: Elicit sacrifice from the capability side rather than the portfolio side.

text: Whose customers are these today, and what do those customers do instead of buying from you?
intent: Establish the real comparison set, including substitutes and doing nothing.

text: You have said you will be better. Better than whom, at what, and in whose judgement?
intent: Convert an absolute claim into the comparative claim it has to be.

text: Your strongest competitor reads this strategy on Monday. What do they do - and why does that not undo you?
intent: Force a specific competitive response into the logic.

text: If a competitor wanted to copy this, what would they have to give up to do it?
intent: Test whether the barrier to imitation is a trade-off or merely a head start.

text: You have said they could copy it but would not want to. Why not, in terms of their interests rather than your hopes?
intent: Test a restraint assumption against the competitor's own incentives.

text: What would have to happen for this advantage to be worth much less in three years - and who inside would notice first?
intent: Test whether advantage is treated as something to be renewed rather than as a permanent barrier.

text: What questions is your organisation working on that your competitors are not asking yet?
intent: Locate the attention and learning that would keep an advantage alive.

text: Does this get you to a materially different position, or to a better version of where you already stand?
intent: Test whether the move is large enough to reach a different peak.

text: What can these pilots prove, what can they structurally never prove, and which decision are they meant to unlock?
intent: Distinguish testing a barrier from substituting pilots for a choice.

text: What do you have to be genuinely better at than anyone else for this way of winning to hold?
intent: Elicit capabilities from the logic rather than from an inventory of current strengths.

text: Which of these capabilities would become pointless if you changed your way of winning?
intent: Test whether capabilities are tied to the strategy or generically desirable.

text: Which of these does every competent competitor already have to do, and which are the few that would actually set you apart?
intent: Separate table stakes from distinctive capability so investment can concentrate.

text: Which two of these capabilities only work because of each other?
intent: Look for a reinforcing system, which is the practical source of durability.

text: Which of these have you never demonstrated you can do? What makes you confident you can build it in the time you have?
intent: Surface assumed capability, a common late-surfacing point of failure.

text: For each gap: are you building it, buying it, partnering for it, or quietly hoping? Who owns it and by when?
intent: Convert an implicit gap into an owned route, or expose that there is none.

text: If one capability gap were going to kill this strategy, which would it be?
intent: Rank the gaps by risk, feeding directly into the barriers to choice.

text: What is different on Monday morning because of this strategy - which measure, which budget line, which standing meeting?
intent: Test whether any mechanism exists to make the choices binding on ordinary behaviour.

text: Which observable thing would move first if this were working - and which if it were quietly failing?
intent: Derive leading indicators from the strategy's own logic.

text: Take your least believed assumption. What could you watch, this quarter, that would tell you whether it is holding?
intent: Attach an observable indicator to each critical condition.

text: What is being defunded or stopped to pay for this? If the answer is efficiencies, what specifically stops?
intent: Test whether resources actually move, since that is the operative strategy.

text: If I looked at last year's spending and your leadership team's calendar, what strategy would I conclude you were running?
intent: Compare the stated strategy with the one the organisation is actually resourcing.

text: Who owns each of these choices, and what are they free to decide without coming back to you?
intent: Test whether decision rights have been chartered or left to default.

text: When a decision comes up that this strategy did not anticipate, who makes it and what do they use to decide?
intent: Test whether the strategy governs the ongoing stream of choices, not just the named ones.

text: Which two or three questions will you now ask of every proposal that comes to you, without exception?
intent: Use the questions leaders reliably ask as a practical lever on culture and behaviour.

text: Set aside whether this is true for a moment. What would have to be true - about your customers, your competitors, your capabilities, your channel, and the economics - for this to be a great choice?
intent: The central move: reverse-engineer the logic so the conditions can be examined without anyone having to defend a position.

text: Are those written as things about the world that could turn out false, or as things you intend to do?
intent: Push must-be-trues from intentions into falsifiable claims.

text: Of all those conditions, which one do you believe least?
intent: Identify the barrier to choice, on which the decision actually turns.

text: Who on your team is most sceptical about this, and which specific condition are they sceptical about?
intent: Locate disagreement on a condition rather than on the conclusion, where it becomes usable.

text: What is that sceptic seeing that makes their view reasonable? What would have to be true for them to be right?
intent: Turn disagreement into a second possibility rather than an obstacle.

text: What is the cheapest thing you could do that would genuinely change your mind about that condition - and what result would count as failing?
intent: Design a decisive test with criteria set in advance.

text: Suppose no further analysis were possible. What would you choose, and when?
intent: Break the deferral pattern and expose whether analysis is buying a decision or delaying one.

text: Looking at the analysis behind this: what result would have led you to a different recommendation?
intent: Test whether the analysis was decision-relevant or decorative.

text: What was the second genuinely different possibility - one that would have put you in a different arena - and what would have had to be true for it to win?
intent: Test whether a choice was made among alternatives or a preferred answer was justified.

text: You have two options in tension. Rather than picking one, what would an option look like that kept the best of both - and what would have to be true for it to work?
intent: Use the tension between options generatively instead of settling it by seniority.

text: You are assuming another party behaves a certain way. Why would they do that if they were purely serving their own interests?
intent: Test each assumption about outside behaviour against that party's incentives.

text: You have said customers should value this. What if they simply do not - does anything in the strategy still work?
intent: Expose logic resting on how others ought to behave.

text: What would you have to see, and by when, to conclude this strategy is wrong rather than just early?
intent: Pre-agree disconfirming evidence so adaptation is a decision rather than a crisis.

text: Last time results disappointed, was the conclusion that the strategy was wrong or that execution was poor? How would you tell the difference next time?
intent: Detect a strategy made unfalsifiable by attributing every shortfall to delivery.

text: What had to be true when your current course was originally set? Which of those conditions still hold?
intent: The unsticking move: reopen the logic of the existing choice rather than generating new ideas on top of it.

text: Without the document in front of you, how would you say the strategy out loud - who you serve, where you play, how you win, and what you have ruled out?
intent: Test sayability, which determines whether the strategy can guide daily choices.

text: Who else in the organisation could say that, in their own words? What would someone two levels down tell me the strategy is?
intent: Test whether the strategy exists beyond the group that wrote it.

text: Pick one function. What does it now choose differently, and what does it stop doing, because of this strategy?
intent: Test whether the strategy cascades into real choices at the level below.

text: Would that function's plan look any different under a completely different corporate strategy? If not, has it made a choice?
intent: Expose functional plans that are unaffected by the enterprise strategy.

text: Where in the organisation will this strategy meet the most resistance, and what will that resistance be protecting?
intent: Anticipate where inherited logic and interests will pull the choices back.

text: Who needs to hear this first, and what is the one thing you need them to be able to repeat afterwards?
intent: Force compression of the strategy to its load-bearing claim.

text: Having gone through this, what is the one thing you are now least sure about?
intent: Let the user name their own priority for the next round rather than being handed one.

text: What is the one conversation you need to have, and with whom, before this can move forward?
intent: Convert the assessment into an owned next step without prescribing the content.
